newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's AIDS scandal-hit Green Cross in takeover.
newsitem.headline: Japan's AIDS scandal-hit Green Cross in takeover.

text.p: Japan's scandal-tainted drug maker Green Cross Corp said on Monday it will be taken over by another Japanese pharmaceuticals firm in a stock swap.

The Osaka-based Green Cross has been at the centre of a scandal concerning HIV-tainted blood products after former Green Cross executives were indicted last October on charges of professional negligence.
Green Cross will be merged into Yoshitomi Pharmaceutical Industries, a medium-sized Japanese drug company.
Under the merger, to take effect on October 1, five shares of Green Cross will be exchanged for three Yoshitomi shares.
Green Cross has seen a sharp fall in sales after public outrage over the scandal prompting boycotts of its products at many medical institutions.
The new company will take over responsibility for any compensation to victims of the tainted blood products, officials said.
Green Cross faces compensation payments totalling about 24 billion yen ($196 million) to people who were infected with HIV through the use of its blood products.
The blood products were not heat-treated even though company documents showed that officials knew there was a risk that such unheated products could be infected with the virus that causes AIDS.
Yoshitomi's president Masashi Goya will take the helm of the new company, while Green Cross president Kazunari Doi will assume the position of executive vice president.
The merged company is expected to have sales of 150 billion yen ($1.22 billion) and parent current profit of 14.5 billion yen ($118 million) in the year ending in March 1998, they said.
Doi said that the worst has passed for the company, with the effect of the angry boycotts peaking in December.

Earlier this month, Green Cross and U.S. -based Chiron Corp said Green Cross will provide an additional $4 million this year to expand human clinical studies of their immunotherapeutic HIV drug, HIV-IT(V).
But the company had said that it expected to post losses in the 1997/98 business year.

The two firms stressed the bright side of the merger, saying that the new company would be able to compete with top Japanese drug makers in the international arena, since Green Cross has a relatively strong overseas operation while Yoshitomi has a firm business base in the domestic market.
They said they would be able to restructure themselves by merging their own networks of research labs, factories and marketing offices.

However, analysts said that, while the merger will help Green Cross prop itself up from the aftermath of the HIV-tainted blood product scandal which broke out last year, advantages for Yoshitomi are not all clear.
"Its hard to see immediately how Yoshitomi would merit from the merger as Green Cross is losing money due to the boycotts," said Mitsuo Ohmi, analyst at Smith Barney International Inc.
Yoshihiko Yamamoto, analyst at Salomon Brothers Asia Ltd, pointed out that the merger may put an end to the boycott and help Green Cross return to profitability.
"The merger will likely give reason for hospitals to end the Green Cross boycott as it would solve the image-problem," he said.
Yoshitomi Pharmaceutical, affiliated with the industry leader Takeda Chemical Industries Co, is the 17th largest Japanese drug maker in terms of sales.
Green Cross shares closed up 36 yen at 566 on Monday, while Yoshitomi shares were down 10 yen at 890.
